chunks: He said: Abul Hasan Ali ibn Malik al-Nahwi reported to me, who said: Muhammad ibn al-Fadhl al-Katib narrated to me, who said: Isa ibn Humaid narrated to us, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah al-Rabi’i saying: al-Asma’i narrated to us, who said:

I entered Basra, and while I was walking along its street, I saw a maid with the most beautiful face among people, yet she looked like a worn-out skin bag. I kept following her while restraining myself until she reached the graveyard and sat beside a grave. Then she began to speak in a voice barely audible:

"This, by Allah, is the true abode, not that with which we deceive ourselves. This, by Allah, separates the loved ones and brings the Reckoning closer; and through it, mercy is known from punishment. O father! May Allah widen your grave and bless you with what He blessed your Prophet. Indeed, I will not say what contradicts what I know: I knew you as generous — when you came, you came as a comfort; and when relied upon, you were a pillar."

Then she said: "I wish I knew how decomposition has changed you / Or how the beauty of your face has become in the dust / For God, how excellent! What an elderly man they buried / Under the stones, neither felt nor seen / Sagacious and forbearing, with resolutions adorned / By bravery and generosity when guests arrive / Since you were moved to the graveyard and decay / Anxieties drew near and sleep fled from my eyes."
And may Allah bless our master Muhammad the Prophet and his immaculate progeny, and grant him abundant peace.

key_terms.البلى: Decomposition, decay — the process of bodily deterioration after death
key_terms.الجنادل: Large stones — the stones covering the grave
key_terms.الكرى: Sleep — poetic term for slumber, lost due to grief
key_terms.المسكن: The abode/dwelling — here referring to the grave as the true dwelling place

ai.seo_question: What did al-Asma’i witness at the graveyard in Basra?
ai.summary: Al-Asma’i, the renowned Arab philologist, narrates witnessing a beautiful but physically worn maid in Basra who visits her father’s grave. She delivers an eloquent lamentation reflecting on death as the true abode and the transitory nature of worldly life, praising her father’s generosity, steadfastness, and hospitality, then recites poetry mourning his loss. The text belongs to the literary tradition (adab) within al-Mufid’s Amali, illustrating how even common people could articulate profound reflections on mortality and the afterlife.

en.mulla-asgharali-m-m-jaffer: 7. He said: Abul Hasan ‘Ali ibn Malik al-Nahwy reported to me from Muhammad ibn al-Fadhl al-Katib, who reported from Isa ibn Hamid, who said: I heard Abu Abdillah al-Rabee saying that it has been reported from al-Asmaee’, who said:

Once I entered al-Basra and as I was walking along, I saw a very beautiful maid looking like a worn-out skin bag. I followed her with constraint, till she reached the graveyard and sat near a grave. Then, with a voice hardly audible, she said:

"This is the abode, not like the one with which we deceive ourselves. By Allah, it is a place, which throws the lovers asunder and brings the Day of Reckoning closer; by which His grace will be known from His chastisement. O father! May Allah widen your grave and bless you with what your Prophet was blessed. As for me, I will not say against what I know! I knew you a generous, comforting whenever you came, fully reliable."

Then she said: "I wish I knew how decomposition has changed you, Or what the beauty of your face has become in the dust! What a nice person! (Do they know which) elderly man they hid under the stones, that he is neither felt nor seen. Sagacious, forbearing, with the resolutions matched by bravery, bountiful when called upon to entertain; Since, you were moved to the graveyard and decay, Anxieties have come closer and my eyes have lost sleep!"
And may Allah bless our master Muhammad, the Prophet and his immaculate progeny.
